claim: mRNA transcription in dsRNA viruses is a highly regulated process.
source: mRNA transcription in dsRNA viruses is a highly regulated process but the mechanism of this regulation is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about dsRNA viruses.

claim: The mechanism of regulation of mRNA transcription in dsRNA viruses is not known.
source: mRNA transcription in dsRNA viruses is a highly regulated process but the mechanism of this regulation is not known.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Six high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus with bound ligands were obtained at 2.9–3.1 Å resolution.
source: Here, by nucleoside triphosphatase (NTPase) assay and comparisons of six high-resolution (2.9–3.1 Å) cryo-electron microscopy structures of cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus with bound ligands, we show that the large sub-domain of the guanylyltransferase (GTase) domain of the turret protein (TP) also has an ATP-binding site and is likely an ATPase.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the resolution range and number of structures obtained.

claim: The large sub-domain of the guanylyltransferase (GTase) domain of the turret protein (TP) has an ATP-binding site.
source: Here, by nucleoside triphosphatase (NTPase) assay and comparisons of six high-resolution (2.9–3.1 Å) cryo-electron microscopy structures of cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus with bound ligands, we show that the large sub-domain of the guanylyltransferase (GTase) domain of the turret protein (TP) also has an ATP-binding site and is likely an ATPase.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by structural data.

claim: The large sub-domain of the GTase domain of the turret protein is likely an ATPase.
source: Here, by nucleoside triphosphatase (NTPase) assay and comparisons of six high-resolution (2.9–3.1 Å) cryo-electron microscopy structures of cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus with bound ligands, we show that the large sub-domain of the guanylyltransferase (GTase) domain of the turret protein (TP) also has an ATP-binding site and is likely an ATPase.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by NTPase assay and structural data.

claim: S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) acts as a signal and binds the methylase-2 domain of TP.
source: S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) acts as a signal and binds the methylase-2 domain of TP to induce conformational change of the viral capsid, which in turn activates the putative ATPase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing SAM binding to MT-2.

claim: SAM binding to the methylase-2 domain induces conformational change of the viral capsid.
source: S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) acts as a signal and binds the methylase-2 domain of TP to induce conformational change of the viral capsid, which in turn activates the putative ATPase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons between S-CPV and unliganded CPV.

claim: Conformational change of the viral capsid activates the putative ATPase.
source: S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) acts as a signal and binds the methylase-2 domain of TP to induce conformational change of the viral capsid, which in turn activates the putative ATPase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: ATP binding/hydrolysis leads to an enlarged capsid for efficient mRNA synthesis.
source: ATP binding/hydrolysis leads to an enlarged capsid for efficient mRNA synthesis, an open GTase domain for His217-mediated guanylyl transfer, and an open methylase-1 domain for SAM binding and methyl transfer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons showing capsid expansion in t-CPV.

claim: ATP binding/hydrolysis leads to an open GTase domain for His217-mediated guanylyl transfer.
source: ATP binding/hydrolysis leads to an enlarged capsid for efficient mRNA synthesis, an open GTase domain for His217-mediated guanylyl transfer, and an open methylase-1 domain for SAM binding and methyl transfer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing GTase domain opening.

claim: ATP binding/hydrolysis leads to an open methylase-1 domain for SAM binding and methyl transfer.
source: ATP binding/hydrolysis leads to an enlarged capsid for efficient mRNA synthesis, an open GTase domain for His217-mediated guanylyl transfer, and an open methylase-1 domain for SAM binding and methyl transfer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing MT-1 domain opening and SAM binding.

claim: Viral transcription is highly regulated in viruses of the Reoviridae.
source: Viral transcription is highly regulated, as demonstrated biochemically in viruses of the Reoviridae (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Furuichi, 1974, 1978; Borsa et al., 1981; Farsetta et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: mRNA transcription in reoviruses is activated by removal of their outer shell in multi-shelled reoviruses.
source: mRNA transcription in these viruses is activated by external actions, for example, removal of their outer shell in multi-shelled reoviruses (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Borsa et al., 1981; Farsetta et al., 2000) and binding of S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) in the single-shelled cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus (CPV) (Furuichi, 1974, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: mRNA transcription in CPV is activated by binding of S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM).
source: mRNA transcription in these viruses is activated by external actions, for example, removal of their outer shell in multi-shelled reoviruses (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Borsa et al., 1981; Farsetta et al., 2000) and binding of S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) in the single-shelled cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus (CPV) (Furuichi, 1974, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Viruses in the Reoviridae contain 9–12 segments of dsRNA enclosed within an inner core.
source: Viruses in the Reoviridae contain 9–12 segments of dsRNA enclosed within an inner core that is a self-competent molecular machine fully capable of RNA transcription and processing (Mertens et al., 2004; Zhou, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The inner core of Reoviridae viruses is a self-competent molecular machine fully capable of RNA transcription and processing.
source: Viruses in the Reoviridae contain 9–12 segments of dsRNA enclosed within an inner core that is a self-competent molecular machine fully capable of RNA transcription and processing (Mertens et al., 2004; Zhou, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Each of the 9–12 dsRNA segments wraps around an RdRP located underneath an icosahedral vertex.
source: Each of the 9–12 dsRNA segments wraps around an RdRP located underneath an icosahedral vertex and can undergo independent and simultaneous RNA transcription within an intact core (i.e., endogenous RNA transcription) (Smith and Furuichi, 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Each dsRNA segment can undergo independent and simultaneous RNA transcription within an intact core.
source: Each of the 9–12 dsRNA segments wraps around an RdRP located underneath an icosahedral vertex and can undergo independent and simultaneous RNA transcription within an intact core (i.e., endogenous RNA transcription) (Smith and Furuichi, 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: CPV has been used as a model system for viral RNA transcription and high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy studies.
source: The simplest of these, the single-shelled CPV (Zhou, 2008) has been used as a model system for viral RNA transcription and high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) studies, as highlighted by the discovery of mRNA cap structures (Furuichi, 1974; Furuichi and Miura, 1975) and the demonstration of near atomic resolution cryoEM (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: mRNA cap structures were discovered in CPV.
source: The simplest of these, the single-shelled CPV (Zhou, 2008) has been used as a model system for viral RNA transcription and high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) studies, as highlighted by the discovery of mRNA cap structures (Furuichi, 1974; Furuichi and Miura, 1975) and the demonstration of near atomic resolution cryoEM (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The atomic models of liganded CPV contain two conformers of the capsid shell proteins (CSP-A and CSP-B).
source: Like the atomic model of unliganded CPV (Yu et al., 2011), the atomic models of these liganded CPV all contain two conformers of the capsid shell proteins (CSP-A and CSP-B), two conformers of the large protrusion proteins (LPP-3 and LPP-5), and one conformer of TP in each asymmetrical unit (e.g., Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structural models.

claim: The atomic models of liganded CPV contain two conformers of the large protrusion proteins (LPP-3 and LPP-5).
source: Like the atomic model of unliganded CPV (Yu et al., 2011), the atomic models of these liganded CPV all contain two conformers of the capsid shell proteins (CSP-A and CSP-B), two conformers of the large protrusion proteins (LPP-3 and LPP-5), and one conformer of TP in each asymmetrical unit (e.g., Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structural models.

claim: The atomic models of liganded CPV contain one conformer of TP in each asymmetrical unit.
source: Like the atomic model of unliganded CPV (Yu et al., 2011), the atomic models of these liganded CPV all contain two conformers of the capsid shell proteins (CSP-A and CSP-B), two conformers of the large protrusion proteins (LPP-3 and LPP-5), and one conformer of TP in each asymmetrical unit (e.g., Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structural models.

claim: In S-CPV, one SAM binds to the MT-2 domain of each TP.
source: In S-CPV, one SAM binds to the MT-2 domain of each TP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In G-CPV, one GTP binds to the GTase site of GTase domain.
source: In G-CPV, one GTP binds to the GTase site of GTase domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In SG-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains.
source: In SG-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains, one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one GTP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In SG-CPV, one Mg2+-GTP binds to the GTase site.
source: In SG-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains, one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one GTP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In SG-CPV, one GTP binds to the putative ATPase site.
source: In SG-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains, one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one GTP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In t-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains.
source: In t-CPV and SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains (Zhu et al., 2014), one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one ATP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In t-CPV, one Mg2+-GTP binds to the GTase site.
source: In t-CPV and SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains (Zhu et al., 2014), one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one ATP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In t-CPV, one ATP binds to the putative ATPase site.
source: In t-CPV and SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains (Zhu et al., 2014), one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one ATP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains.
source: In t-CPV and SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains (Zhu et al., 2014), one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one ATP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In SGA-CPV, one Mg2+-GTP binds to the GTase site.
source: In t-CPV and SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains (Zhu et al., 2014), one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one ATP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In SGA-CPV, one ATP binds to the putative ATPase site.
source: In t-CPV and SGA-CPV, two SAM molecules bind to the MT-1 and MT-2 domains (Zhu et al., 2014), one Mg2+-GTP to the GTase site and one ATP to the putative ATPase site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The capsid shell of S-CPV is slightly expanded with a non-uniform outwards movement of all structure proteins compared to unliganded CPV.
source: Superposition of the structures (both at 3.1 Å resolution) of S-CPV and the unliganded CPV (Yu et al., 2011) shows that the capsid shell of S-CPV is slightly expanded with a non-uniform outwards movement of all structure proteins (Figure 2A,B, Video 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: The apical domain of CSP-A in S-CPV has the largest movement of ∼1 Å compared to unliganded CPV.
source: For example, the apical domain of CSP-A, located next to the fivefold axis, has the largest movement of ∼1 Å (RMSD: 0.97 Å); the dimerization domain, located near the twofold axis, has the smallest movement of ∼0.5 Å (RMSD: 0.49 Å); the CPV-unique small protrusion domain, which is located between the apical and the dimerization domain, moves outwards ∼0.8 Å (RMSD: 0.83 Å) (Figure 2A and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The dimerization domain of CSP-A in S-CPV has the smallest movement of ∼0.5 Å compared to unliganded CPV.
source: For example, the apical domain of CSP-A, located next to the fivefold axis, has the largest movement of ∼1 Å (RMSD: 0.97 Å); the dimerization domain, located near the twofold axis, has the smallest movement of ∼0.5 Å (RMSD: 0.49 Å); the CPV-unique small protrusion domain, which is located between the apical and the dimerization domain, moves outwards ∼0.8 Å (RMSD: 0.83 Å) (Figure 2A and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The CPV-unique small protrusion domain moves outwards ∼0.8 Å in S-CPV compared to unliganded CPV.
source: For example, the apical domain of CSP-A, located next to the fivefold axis, has the largest movement of ∼1 Å (RMSD: 0.97 Å); the dimerization domain, located near the twofold axis, has the smallest movement of ∼0.5 Å (RMSD: 0.49 Å); the CPV-unique small protrusion domain, which is located between the apical and the dimerization domain, moves outwards ∼0.8 Å (RMSD: 0.83 Å) (Figure 2A and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: TP moves outwards ∼1 Å in S-CPV compared to unliganded CPV.
source: TP, residing on the apical domain of CSP-A, moves outwards ∼1 Å (RMSD: 0.99 Å), which is the same as the displacement of the apical domain of CSP-A (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Both MT-1 and MT-2 domains of TP have the typical structural motif of SAM-dependent methyltransferases.
source: Both MT-1 and MT-2 domains of TP have the typical structural motif of SAM-dependent methyltransferases with a seven-stranded β-sheet sandwiched by α-helices (Schluckebier et al., 1995; Hodel et al., 1996; Reinisch et al., 2000; Sutton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Only the MT-2 domain in S-CPV bound SAM.
source: Unexpectedly, only the MT-2 domain in S-CPV bound SAM (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The MT-2 domain structure of S-CPV is indistinguishable from that of the unliganded CPV at 3.1 Å resolution.
source: Except for slight displacement due to the outwards movement of TP as described above, the MT-2 domain structure of S-CPV is indistinguishable from that of the unliganded CPV at the current resolution of 3.1 Å (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: The cryoEM image of t-CPV shows string-like densities emanating from the viral particles.
source: In contrast to that of S-CPV (Figure 3A), the cryoEM image of t-CPV shows string-like densities emanating from the viral particles, which we attribute to newly synthesized mRNA molecules in the process of release from the actively transcribing virions (arrows in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The string-like densities in t-CPV images are attributed to newly synthesized mRNA molecules in the process of release from the actively transcribing virions.
source: In contrast to that of S-CPV (Figure 3A), the cryoEM image of t-CPV shows string-like densities emanating from the viral particles, which we attribute to newly synthesized mRNA molecules in the process of release from the actively transcribing virions (arrows in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on the observed densities.

claim: All domains of TP undergo global outwards movements of ∼9 Å from S-CPV to t-CPV.
source: All domains of TP undergo global outwards movements (∼9 Å), while only the MT-1 domain and the large sub-domain of GTase domain of TP exhibit local conformation changes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: Only the MT-1 domain and the large sub-domain of GTase domain of TP exhibit local conformation changes from S-CPV to t-CPV.
source: All domains of TP undergo global outwards movements (∼9 Å), while only the MT-1 domain and the large sub-domain of GTase domain of TP exhibit local conformation changes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: CSP-A rotates outwards up to 9 Å around a pivot point near the twofold axis from S-CPV to t-CPV.
source: CSP-A not only rotates outwards (up to 9 Å) around a pivot point near the twofold axis (global domain movements indicated by dashed ellipses in Figure 3D and Video 5), but it also changes conformation in its apical domain (dotted ellipse in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: CSP-A changes conformation in its apical domain from S-CPV to t-CPV.
source: CSP-A not only rotates outwards (up to 9 Å) around a pivot point near the twofold axis (global domain movements indicated by dashed ellipses in Figure 3D and Video 5), but it also changes conformation in its apical domain (dotted ellipse in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: An enlarged capsid would facilitate dsRNA template movement, enabling efficient mRNA synthesis.
source: Since viral mRNA synthesis takes place within the confines of intact virus core, an enlarged capsid would facilitate dsRNA template movement, enabling efficient mRNA synthesis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the Results section.

claim: The t-CPV structure contained two ligands bound to the GTase domain of each TP.
source: The t-CPV structure contained two ligands bound to the GTase domain of each TP (Figure 1D, Video 6 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The first ligand in t-CPV GTase domain is GTP involved in transfer of a guanylyl group catalyzed by GTase.
source: The first is the expected GTP molecule involved in transfer of a guanylyl group catalyzed by GTase and is located at a cleft of the GTase active site (Video 6 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The second ligand in t-CPV GTase domain is bound to the large sub-domain, away from the cleft.
source: The second is unexpected ligand, bound to the large sub-domain, away from the cleft (Video 6 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The density of the unexpected ligand fits very well with the atomic model of an ATP molecule.
source: The density of the unexpected ligand is as strong as that of the GTP bound to the GTase site and the surrounding amino acid residues, and it fits very well with the atomic model of an ATP molecule, suggesting that the large sub-domain of GTase domain of TP could also be a viral ATP-binding site (Figure 4A and Video 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative ATP-binding site is located outside the turret chamber.
source: Located outside the turret chamber (Figures 1D, 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the putative ATP-binding site is inaccessible to both the dsRNA genome and the nascent mRNA, thus rendering it unable to directly participate in the mRNA transcription and the capping reactions but may function as a regulatory protein or enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative ATP-binding site is inaccessible to both the dsRNA genome and the nascent mRNA.
source: Located outside the turret chamber (Figures 1D, 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the putative ATP-binding site is inaccessible to both the dsRNA genome and the nascent mRNA, thus rendering it unable to directly participate in the mRNA transcription and the capping reactions but may function as a regulatory protein or enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative ATP-binding site may function as a regulatory protein or enzyme.
source: Located outside the turret chamber (Figures 1D, 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the putative ATP-binding site is inaccessible to both the dsRNA genome and the nascent mRNA, thus rendering it unable to directly participate in the mRNA transcription and the capping reactions but may function as a regulatory protein or enzyme.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Results section based on structural observations.

claim: The global movements and local conformational changes of structural proteins observed in t-CPV are not a consequence, but rather a trigger of RNA transcription.
source: These results indicate that (1) the global movements and local conformational changes of structural proteins observed in t-CPV are not a consequence, but rather a trigger of RNA transcription; (2) the large sub-domain of the GTase domain binds ATP to mediate the conformational changes observed in t-CPV.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on comparison of SGA-CPV and t-CPV structures.

claim: The large sub-domain of the GTase domain binds ATP to mediate the conformational changes observed in t-CPV.
source: These results indicate that (1) the global movements and local conformational changes of structural proteins observed in t-CPV are not a consequence, but rather a trigger of RNA transcription; (2) the large sub-domain of the GTase domain binds ATP to mediate the conformational changes observed in t-CPV.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural comparisons.

claim: Part of the loop connecting α13 and α14 in S-CPV became a helix (αC) in SGA-CPV, SG-CPV, and t-CPV.
source: Accompanying these conformational changes, part of the loop connecting α13 and α14 in S-CPV became a helix (αC) in SGA-CPV, SG-CPV, and t-CPV (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The hydrolysis of ATP is required for mRNA synthesis in CPV.
source: Previous biochemical studies have shown that the hydrolysis of ATP is required for mRNA synthesis (Furuichi, 1978) and that efficient synthesis of CPV mRNA depended on the concentrations of SAM and ATP in a synergistic manner (Furuichi, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Efficient synthesis of CPV mRNA depended on the concentrations of SAM and ATP in a synergistic manner.
source: Previous biochemical studies have shown that the hydrolysis of ATP is required for mRNA synthesis (Furuichi, 1978) and that efficient synthesis of CPV mRNA depended on the concentrations of SAM and ATP in a synergistic manner (Furuichi, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: In the absence of SAM, neither GTP nor ATP induced any conformational change in CPV.
source: Our structures of G-CPV and A-CPV show that, in the absence of SAM, neither GTP nor ATP induced any conformational change (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: A GTP bound to the GTase active site in G-CPV.
source: While a GTP bound to the GTase active site in G-CPV (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), neither ATP nor GTP was observed at the newly discovered ATP-binding site in A-CPV and G-CPV (Table 1), indicating that ATP/GTP binding to the large sub-domain of TP GTase domain is directly regulated by SAM, most likely via binding to the MT-2 domain, since the structure of S-CPV revealed only MT-2 domain contained SAM (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Neither ATP nor GTP was observed at the newly discovered ATP-binding site in A-CPV and G-CPV.
source: While a GTP bound to the GTase active site in G-CPV (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), neither ATP nor GTP was observed at the newly discovered ATP-binding site in A-CPV and G-CPV (Table 1), indicating that ATP/GTP binding to the large sub-domain of TP GTase domain is directly regulated by SAM, most likely via binding to the MT-2 domain, since the structure of S-CPV revealed only MT-2 domain contained SAM (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: ATP/GTP binding to the large sub-domain of TP GTase domain is directly regulated by SAM.
source: While a GTP bound to the GTase active site in G-CPV (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), neither ATP nor GTP was observed at the newly discovered ATP-binding site in A-CPV and G-CPV (Table 1), indicating that ATP/GTP binding to the large sub-domain of TP GTase domain is directly regulated by SAM, most likely via binding to the MT-2 domain, since the structure of S-CPV revealed only MT-2 domain contained SAM (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural comparisons.

claim: Phosphate released upon hydrolysis of NTPs depended on the presence of SAM.
source: Phosphate released upon hydrolysis of NTPs indeed depended on the presence of SAM and the most favorable NTP substrate was ATP, with decreasing rate of hydrolysis of other substrates in the order of GTP > CTP > UTP in the presence of SAM (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NTPase assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The most favorable NTP substrate for CPV NTPase was ATP, with decreasing rate of hydrolysis of other substrates in the order of GTP > CTP > UTP in the presence of SAM.
source: Phosphate released upon hydrolysis of NTPs indeed depended on the presence of SAM and the most favorable NTP substrate was ATP, with decreasing rate of hydrolysis of other substrates in the order of GTP > CTP > UTP in the presence of SAM (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NTPase assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mRNA transcription of CPV is SAM-dependent and is specifically coupled to ATP hydrolysis.
source: Previous biochemical studies have shown that the mRNA transcription of CPV is SAM-dependent and is specifically coupled to ATP hydrolysis (Furuichi, 1978, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The removal of turret in orthoreovirus leads to loss of mRNA transcription activity.
source: Additionally, it has been shown that the removal of turret in orthoreovirus leads loss of mRNA transcription activity (Luongo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The ATP-binding site of TP GTase domain is possibly a SAM-dependent ATPase that mediates the activation of mRNA transcription.
source: Our structural results, when combined with these biochemical data, suggest that the ATP-binding site of TP GTase domain is possibly a SAM-dependent ATPase that mediates the activation of mRNA transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: The density for the bound GTP in the GTase site is strong in t-CPV.
source: The density for the bound GTP in the GTase site is strong in t-CPV (Figure 6A, Video 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) but weak in G-CPV, particularly at the triphosphate group (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The density for the bound GTP in the GTase site is weak in G-CPV, particularly at the triphosphate group.
source: The density for the bound GTP in the GTase site is strong in t-CPV (Figure 6A, Video 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) but weak in G-CPV, particularly at the triphosphate group (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The opening leading to the GTase site is widened from 13 to 15 Å in t-CPV compared to G-CPV.
source: Compared to that of G-CPV, the opening (or 'gate') leading to the GTase site and coupled to the putative mRNA releasing hole (Yu et al., 2011) is widened from 13 to 15 Å in t-CPV, likely to accommodate nascent mRNA (Figures 5A, 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: The widening of the gate in t-CPV is likely to accommodate nascent mRNA.
source: Compared to that of G-CPV, the opening (or 'gate') leading to the GTase site and coupled to the putative mRNA releasing hole (Yu et al., 2011) is widened from 13 to 15 Å in t-CPV, likely to accommodate nascent mRNA (Figures 5A, 6A,B).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section.

claim: Extra density next to the β, γ phosphates of the bound GTP in t-CPV is interpreted as coordinated Mg2+.
source: In the open state of GTase domain in t-CPV, we observed extra density next to the β, γ phosphates of the bound GTP (Figure 6A and Video 6), which we interpret as coordinated Mg2+ for two reasons. First, Mg2+ was the only divalent cation in our reaction mixture. Second, the GTase domains in SGA-CPV and SG-CPV are also in the open state with prominent densities attributable to Mg2+ (Figure 6C,D and Video 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data and experimental conditions.

claim: Mg2+ is required for GTase activity of viruses in Reoviridae.
source: Biochemical data have shown that the Mg2+ is required for GTase activity of viruses in Reoviridae (Yamakawa et al., 1982; Le Blois et al., 1992; Martinez-Costas et al., 1995; Qiu and Luongo, 2003; Mohd Jaafar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Only the open state of GTase (with the putative Mg2+) is catalytically active.
source: Biochemical data have shown that the Mg2+ is required for GTase activity of viruses in Reoviridae (Yamakawa et al., 1982; Le Blois et al., 1992; Martinez-Costas et al., 1995; Qiu and Luongo, 2003; Mohd Jaafar et al., 2005). Therefore, only the open state (with the putative Mg2+) is catalytically active.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: The gate opening is achieved through the displacement of α14 (the gate helix).
source: Remarkably, the gate opening is achieved through the displacement of α14 (i.e., the gate helix), one of the three helices comprising the active site of the putative viral ATPase (Figures 4A–C, 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The active sites of the putative ATPase and GTase do not share any amino acids or secondary elements.
source: However, even though the gate helix α14 controls the open and closed state, it is not part of the GTase active site. In fact, the active sites of the putative ATPase and GTase do not share any amino acids or secondary elements (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative ATPase regulates GTase activity allosterically.
source: Therefore, the putative ATPase regulates GTase activity allosterically.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural observations.

claim: The triphosphate moiety of GTP forms only one hydrogen bond in the closed conformation of GTase.
source: The triphosphate moiety forms only one hydrogen bond (between the β phosphate and Tyr59) in the closed conformation (Figure 5A) but forms three or four more hydrogen bonds in the open conformation including the two formed by the α phosphate with His212 and Arg255 (Figure 6A,C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The triphosphate moiety of GTP forms three or four more hydrogen bonds in the open conformation of GTase.
source: The triphosphate moiety forms only one hydrogen bond (between the β phosphate and Tyr59) in the closed conformation (Figure 5A) but forms three or four more hydrogen bonds in the open conformation including the two formed by the α phosphate with His212 and Arg255 (Figure 6A,C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Lys190 of GTase domain in mammalian reovirus is responsible for guanylylation of GTases.
source: Previous loss-of-function mutagenesis study of lysine residues in mammalian reovirus suggested that Lys190 of GTase domain is responsible for guanylylation of GTases (Luongo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The conserved β strands (β3 and β4) in CPV GTase is connected by a segment of only 13 aa (a loop from residues 166–178), which contains no lysine.
source: Surprisingly, the conserved β strands (β3 and β4) in CPV GTPase is connected by a segment of only 13 aa (a loop from residues 166–178), which contains no lysine (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The only lysine residue in CPV GTase domain within the vicinity of the bound GTP is Lys234.
source: Within the vicinity of the bound GTP, the only lysine residue in CPV GTase domain is Lys234, which maps to a non-conserved residue (Ser259) in mammalian reovirus GTase domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: During GTase transition from its closed to open state, the α phosphorus of the GTP moves towards a histidine-rich segment and away from Lys234.
source: Moreover, during GTase transition from its closed to open state, the α phosphorus of the GTP moves towards a histidine-rich segment and away from Lys234 (Figures 6, 7 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Lys234 cannot directly participate in guanylylation of GTase.
source: Therefore, our structures indicate that Lys234 cannot directly participate in guanylylation of GTase, a conclusion that is contrary to a previous suggestion based on a likely incorrect placement of a GMP molecule in the active site in a poorer resolution map (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural data.

claim: The histidine-rich segment contains two histidines (His208 and His217) that are conserved in orthoreovirus and aquareovirus.
source: By contrast, the histidine-rich segment contains two histidines (His208 and His217) that are either hydrogen bonded to or in proximity with the α- or β-phosphate of the bound GTP in the open state of CPV GTase (Figure 6A,C,D) and conserved in both the orthoreovirus (Reinisch et al., 2000) and aquareovirus (Zhang et al., 2010b) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: His208 is not the active site residue; rather, it stabilizes the charge built up on the β-phosphate in the transition state during the catalysis process.
source: Located on the same side of the leaving group (i.e., β, γ-diphosphate), His208 is hydrogen bonded to the β-phosphate of the GTP in SGA-CPV and SG-CPV. Therefore, His208 is not the active site residue; rather, it stabilizes the charge built up on the β-phosphate in the transition state during the catalysis process.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural data.

claim: His217 is likely the active site residue for guanylyl transfer.
source: Instead, His217 is likely the active site residue. His217 and the leaving group are on opposite sides of the α phosphorus, a geometry suitable for in-line nucleophilic attack of the α phosphorus by His217 (Figures 6, 7 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural data.

claim: The two conserved histidine residues in orthoreovirus are required for the GTase activities.
source: Indeed, these two conserved histidine residues in orthoreovirus are required for the GTase activities (Qiu and Luongo, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: GTases of viruses in the Reoviridae family have maximum activity at pH about or lower than the pKa value (∼6.0) of histidine.
source: Furthermore, unlike KxDG GTases that have maximum activity at high pH, GTases of viruses in the Reoviridae family have maximum activity at pH about or lower than the pKa value (∼6.0) of histidine (Qiu and Luongo, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Enzyme guanylylation mediated by His217 is likely the rate-limiting step in the process of guanylyl transfer.
source: Because we observed only the pre guanylylation state of GTase in all three CPV structures (t-CPV, SGA-CPV, and SG-CPV), we reason that enzyme guanylylation mediated by His217 is likely the rate-limiting step in the process of guanylyl transfer.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural observations.

claim: The putative viral ATPase regulates the methyl transfer activity of MT-1 through a long-range allosteric effect.
source: Our structures also indicate that the putative viral ATPase regulates the methyl transfer activity of MT-1 through a long-range allosteric effect (Figures 1D, 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on structural data.

claim: The distance from the putative ATPase site to the MT-1 in the same molecule is ∼80 Å.
source: First of all, active sites of MT-1 and the putative ATPase are spatially separated from each other (Figure 1D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1) as the distance from the putative ATPase site to the MT-1 in the same molecule is ∼80 Å, while that to a neighboring MT-1 is ∼40 Å (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The distance from the putative ATPase site to a neighboring MT-1 is ∼40 Å.
source: First of all, active sites of MT-1 and the putative ATPase are spatially separated from each other (Figure 1D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1) as the distance from the putative ATPase site to the MT-1 in the same molecule is ∼80 Å, while that to a neighboring MT-1 is ∼40 Å (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: MT-1 remains incapable of SAM binding in S-CPV even if the putative ATPase is activated by SAM but lacks ATP for binding/hydrolysis.
source: Second, even if the putative ATPase is activated by SAM but lacks ATP for binding/hydrolysis, MT-1 remains incapable of SAM binding as was observed in S-CPV.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: MT-1 becomes SAM bound in t-CPV where ATP is available.
source: In t-CPV where ATP is available, MT-1 becomes SAM bound (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Two loops lining one side of the un-occupied MT-1 active site in S-CPV shifted up to 4 Å in t-CPV.
source: In particular, two loops lining one side of the un-occupied MT-1 active site in S-CPV shifted up to 4 Å in t-CPV, resulting in an enlarged active site to accommodate the SAM molecule required for methyl transfer (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The shift of loops in MT-1 results in an enlarged active site to accommodate the SAM molecule required for methyl transfer.
source: In particular, two loops lining one side of the un-occupied MT-1 active site in S-CPV shifted up to 4 Å in t-CPV, resulting in an enlarged active site to accommodate the SAM molecule required for methyl transfer (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The structures of MT-1 domains with bound SAM in SGA-CPV and SG-CPV are essentially identical to those in t-CPV.
source: In SGA-CPV and SG-CPV, the structures of MT-1 domains with bound SAM are essentially identical to those in t-CPV (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), though the outwards movement of MT-1 in SG-CPV is ∼1.1 Å less (Figure 8E), likely due to the lower rate of GTP hydrolysis by the ATPase (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative viral ATPase has the conserved structural motif for recognition of the adenine base of ATP.
source: This putative viral ATPase has the conserved structural motif for recognition of the adenine base of ATP: hydrogen bonds between the side chains of Ser301, Asp302 and Tyr316 and the adenine ring, pi–pi stacking between the side chain of Tyr305 with the adenine base, and the cation–pi stacking between the side chain of Arg271 and the adenine base (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative viral ATPase lacks the structural motifs of canonical nucleoside triphosphatases (NTPases), most notably the P loop.
source: However, this putative viral ATPase lacks the structural motifs of canonical nucleoside triphosphatases (NTPases) (including cellular kinases), most notably the P loop, for binding the phosphoryl moiety of NTP (Saraste et al., 1990; Smith and Rayment, 1996; Snider and Houry, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: The phosphoryl group of the bound ATP is stabilized through hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Arg271 or Tyr268 from α13 helix.
source: Instead, the phosphoryl group of the bound ATP is stabilized through hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Arg271 or Tyr268 from α13 helix (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative ATPase active site is composed of three consecutive helices of α13, α14, and α15.
source: Although the large sub-domain has an α helices/β sheet fold, the putative viral ATPase active site is composed of three consecutive helices of α13, α14, and α15 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: The putative ATPase is structurally different from all ATPase known to date, and it may represent a new type of ATPase.
source: Structurally, the putative ATPase is different from all ATPase known to date, and it may thus represent a new type of ATPase.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on structural comparisons.

claim: The triphosphate moiety of the bound ATP is better stabilized by forming two more hydrogen bonds with the protein compared to GTP.
source: More importantly, while the triphosphate group of the bound GTP forms only one hydrogen bond through its β phosphate with Tyr268 of the active site (Figure 4C), the triphosphate moiety of the bound ATP is better stabilized by forming two more hydrogen bonds with the protein (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: The more hydrogen bonded ATP is a more efficient substrate of the putative viral ATPase for hydrolysis than GTP.
source: Conceivably, the more hydrogen bonded ATP is a more efficient substrate of the putative viral ATPase for hydrolysis than GTP, consistent with the colorimetric assay of CPV NTPase activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on structural data and biochemical assay.

claim: CPV senses the entrance into host cytoplasm by detecting the presence of SAM.
source: CPV senses the entrance into host cytoplasm by detecting the presence of SAM.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: SAM binding to MT-2 causes initial conformational change of the virus capsid, which activates the putative viral ATPase.
source: SAM, acting as a signal and binding to its receptor of MT-2, causes initial conformational change of the virus capsid, which activates the putative viral ATPase (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The activated viral ATPase binds and hydrolyzes ATP to cause three major structural transformations.
source: The activated viral ATPase then binds and hydrolyzes ATP to cause three major structural transformations, leading to mRNA transcription and capping (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: As a result of the translocation of CSP, the viral capsid is enlarged, facilitating dsRNA template movement and enabling efficient mRNA synthesis.
source: First, as a result of the translocation of CSP, the viral capsid is enlarged, facilitating dsRNA template movement and enabling efficient mRNA synthesis (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The GTase domain transforms from its closed to open state upon ATP binding/hydrolysis.
source: Second, the GTase domain transforms from its closed to open state (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Only in the open state can the GTase bind Mg2+ and catalyze His217-mediated guanylyl transfer.
source: Although GTP binds to the GTase active site in both states of GTase domain, only in the open state can the GTase bind Mg2+ and catalyze His217-mediated guanylyl transfer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The MT-1 domain transforms from its closed to open conformation upon ATP binding/hydrolysis.
source: Third, the MT-1 domain transforms from its closed to open conformation (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Only in its open conformation can MT-1 bind SAM.
source: Only in its open conformation can MT-1 bind SAM.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The putative ATPase regulates the activity of MT-1 in a neighboring TP, probably through the conformational changes of the putative ATPase sub-domain upon ATP binding/hydrolysis.
source: We, therefore propose that the putative ATPase regulates the activity of MT-1 in a neighboring TP, probably through the conformational changes of the putative ATPase sub-domain upon ATP binding/hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism stated in the Discussion section.

claim: From S-CPV to t-CPV, the C-terminal loop of GTase domain exhibits significant movement towards the MT-1 domain of its neighboring TP molecule.
source: Notably, from S-CPV to t-CPV, the C-terminal loop of GTase domain exhibits significant movement towards the MT-1 domain of its neighboring TP molecule, presumably contributing to open the active site of the MT-1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: Several viruses within the Reoviridae have been shown to have ATPase activity.
source: Several viruses within the Reoviridae, such as rotaviruses and blue-tongue viruses, cause wide spread diseases in human and live stocks. Some of these multi-shelled viruses in the Reoviridae, including the animal reovirus and blue-tongue virus, have been shown to have ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997; Ramadevi and Roy, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Multi-shelled reoviruses may have employed the ATPase-mediated activation for mRNA transcription and capping identified in CPV.
source: The remarkable parallel between the ATPase activity and the transcription activity indicated that they may have also employed the ATPase-mediated activation for mRNA transcription and capping identified here.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section based on parallels with CPV.

claim: Reovirus cores had high level of ATPase activity.
source: For example, reovirus cores had high level of ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Banerjee and Shatkin, 1970; Drayna and Fields, 1982; Farsetta et al., 2000), but virions had little ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could not synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Farsetta et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Reovirus cores could synthesize mRNA.
source: For example, reovirus cores had high level of ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Banerjee and Shatkin, 1970; Drayna and Fields, 1982; Farsetta et al., 2000), but virions had little ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could not synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Farsetta et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Reovirus virions had little ATPase activity.
source: For example, reovirus cores had high level of ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Banerjee and Shatkin, 1970; Drayna and Fields, 1982; Farsetta et al., 2000), but virions had little ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could not synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Farsetta et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Reovirus virions could not synthesize mRNA.
source: For example, reovirus cores had high level of ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Banerjee and Shatkin, 1970; Drayna and Fields, 1982; Farsetta et al., 2000), but virions had little ATPase activity (Noble and Nibert, 1997) and could not synthesize mRNA (Shatkin and Sipe, 1968; Farsetta et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: It is the removal of outer shell other than SAM that triggers the activation process in multi-shelled reoviruses.
source: Thus, it is the removal of outer shell other than SAM that triggers the activation process in multi-shelled reoviruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on comparison with CPV.
